title: Detection of Establish Accounts
summary: This detection strategy covers account establishment, where an adversary creates the email, cloud and service accounts that carry a later operation. It matters because these accounts sit at the centre of phishing, data staging and command and control, and because signup behaviour is one of the few places where infrastructure preparation becomes visible to defenders. The telemetry that makes it possible includes provider signup and audit logs, single sign on provisioning records with source address and device, and mail gateway entries for new sending domains. The strategy fails in practice because new accounts are created in huge numbers for good reasons, so the rule must distinguish automation with a change record from bursts that share one source, one naming pattern and one payment method.

beginner.definition: Account establishment means an attacker creates new accounts to use during an attack. They may register free mail accounts, cloud tenants or service logins. This detection looks for the creation and first use of those accounts before they are used against you.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every later step needs an identity the attacker controls. Phishing needs a mailbox. Data theft needs storage. Remote control needs a login. Those accounts leave creation and first use records. If you spot a burst of new accounts from odd sources, you may be seeing the start of a campaign. That warning gives you time to block the source before the attack arrives.
howItWorks: Identity providers and mail services log when an account is created, including the source address, the device and the name chosen.
Those records are collected into your SIEM or reviewed through the provider console.
The rule counts how many accounts appear in a short window from one address, one device or one payment or verification method.
It also checks the name and domain pattern against real company information, looking for lookalike names.
When a burst matches, the alert lists the accounts, the shared attributes and the first sign in of each one.
beginner.example: Think of a library card desk. One person joining is normal. Twenty people joining in ten minutes, all giving the same postal address and all asking for a card in a similar name, is a pattern worth a phone call to the branch manager.
takeaways: Account creation is preparation, so it is worth detecting before the accounts are used.
Volume, shared attributes and lookalike naming are the three strongest signals.
Most of this telemetry lives with the provider, so collection and review must be arranged in advance.

objectives: Explain how attacker controlled accounts support phishing, staging and remote access
Identify the account creation and first use events available from your providers
Describe the shared attributes that reveal a coordinated signup burst
Recognise lookalike domains and names that imitate your organisation
Write a rule that counts new accounts per source address or verification method
dataSources: Cloud identity provider audit logs recording user and service account creation with the acting principal
Mail service or provider signup logs showing the source address, device and verification method used
Domain registration and certificate transparency feed entries for names that resemble your brand
Administrative audit trails from help desk and onboarding systems showing who requested each new account
logic: The pattern is a burst of account creations that share a small set of attributes: the same source address range, the same device fingerprint, sequential names, one payment or verification method, and use within minutes of creation. The fields to correlate are the created account name, the creation timestamp, the source address and the verification or payment identifier. The benign case is onboarding automation, where each account has a ticket, a real manager and a unique device, while the malicious case shows many accounts with no tickets, near identical names and immediate outbound mail from the same small address pool.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Burst of new accounts from one source with no change record
# logsource:
#   product: azure
#   service: audit
# detection:
#   selection:
#     operation: Add user
#     result: success
#   filter:
#     initiator|in: approved_onboarding_service_principals
#   timeframe: 30m
#   condition: selection and not filter | count() by source_ip > 10
# level: medium
falsePositives: A recruitment drive that creates accounts for a large group of new starters on the same morning
An automated onboarding script that provisions lab or training accounts for a workshop
A marketing campaign tool that registers several sender identities from one cloud address
A merger or acquisition that imports hundreds of accounts through a bulk provisioning job
tuningNotes: Allow list the service principals and addresses used by provisioning automation, and require a matching change record for bulk creation before the alert is closed. Baseline normal daily creation counts per tenant so the threshold reflects your business rhythm rather than a fixed number. You lose detection of accounts an attacker creates entirely outside your providers, which is the usual case, so treat this rule as one signal in a wider brand and domain monitoring programme rather than as complete coverage.
